items.title: Slide Hampton interviewed by Monk Rowe, West Orange, New Jersey, July 30, 2003
items.q: when we did the trombone thing recently at the Blue Note with Bobby Burgess and Bill Watrous

ctx.x: To get a rehearsal in and scheduling.

It’s a job. When we did the trombone album, the trombone CD, we did that one thing, but we could never have that same group again. But we had good guys after that too, guys that weren’t on the CD. And when we did the trombone thing recently at the Blue Note with Bobby Burgess and Bill Watrous you know, those guys and Benny Powell, they love to work together so they’ll just about do anything they can to get to work in that group © Fillius Jazz Archive -24-
because they loved being there so much. But in general when you’ve got a group like that it’s hard to get that group together more than once. There always will be some change in there.

items.title: Bill Watrous interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 26, 1999
items.q: I will relate to you what I’ve been told by people like Wayne Andre and others... you’ve got firstly let’s start for instance with J.J. for instance and Curtis Fuller and Slide Hampton. Okay, which are icons amongst themselves

ctx.x: Yeah, thank you. Where do you put yourself?

I will relate to you what I’ve been told by people like Wayne Andre and others. I’m sort of a, if you look down the list of modern trombone players you’ve got firstly let’s start for instance with J.J. for instance and Curtis Fuller and Slide Hampton. Okay, which are icons amongst themselves, and then Jimmy Cleveland sort of falls in the slot there. And then we look at Frankie Rosolino and Urbie and Carl. And I sort of fall in there sort of after those guys somewhere. I’m sort of a, I would say people consider me…
What kind of music do you like to listen to at home?

items.title: Slide Hampton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Recently you recorded one, Manchester Craftsman’s Guild, with Bill Watrous as your guest.

ctx.x: Recently you recorded one, Manchester Craftsman’s Guild, with Bill Watrous as your guest. Does anybody play higher than Bill Watrous?

[laughs] I don’t know. But I think his objective is not to play high. Bill’s objective is to play beautiful. He plays melodies really beautifully. That’s his thing. There’s a guy in Canada that plays so high on trombone, but when he plays high, he’s very accurate.
